tier_reason: Independent measurement by the asio_kcp author (not the KCP author) with public test code (libinzhangyuan/enet_bench_test, asio_kcp tag kcp_bench_mark_test) and public raw logs, run concurrently against ENet on the same machine and path; no compiler, flags, CPU or loss rate, and it is an informal one-off internet run rather than a reproducible lab setup, so B and not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Wiki excerpt of a worst-network-lag moment (timestamp 10:51.21): asio_kcp 291 295 269 268 231 195 249 230 225 204 versus enet 1563 1520 1470 1482 1438 1454 1412 1637 1588 1540 (mean about 246 vs about 1,510 ms, roughly 6x lower, derived from page data). The wiki and bench_mark.md text says 'The lag is less than 1 second when network lag happen. 3 times better than enet when lag happen.' Over the full public logs of the concurrent 500-byte run (enet_bench_test/bench_mark_log/enet_500.log and kcp_500.log, about 16:18 to 16:30): ENet mean 285 ms, p99 3,911 ms, max 8,179 ms vs KCP mean 126 ms, p99 574 ms, max 1,013 ms, but median ENet 62 ms vs KCP 80 ms (derived from page data). README claim vs TCP (first-party, no data): 30%-40% lower average latency and three times lower maximum latency at the cost of 10%-20% more bandwidth.
corrections.caveats: Independent measurement (asio_kcp author, libinzhangyuan/reliable_udp_bench_mark bench_mark.md) but an informal one-off run on a real internet path from a home WiFi/ADSL client to an internet server: no compiler, flags, CPU model or loss rate, units are not printed (milliseconds, consistent with the 50 ms send interval), and the wiki numbers are a pasted 10-sample log excerpt from one bad-network moment whose timestamp does not appear in the public enet_bench_test logs. The full public logs show KCP wins on tail latency (p99 574 vs 3,911 ms, max 1,013 vs 8,179 ms) but ENet has the lower median (62 vs 80 ms), so the win is tail latency under loss, not typical latency. ENet's ENET_PEER_DEFAULT_ROUND_TRIP_TIME was changed from 500 to 50 for the test. The wiki's own wording is '3 times better than enet', not 'more than three times'. The TCP claim in the README is first-party percentages with no public data in the repo. Recent commits (2026-06-19 to 2026-06-23) are README edits; the protocol code is stable. Category dns-quic-http3 is a loose fit: KCP is a generic reliable-UDP ARQ, not QUIC or HTTP/3.

notes: Wiki and linked bench_mark.md confirm the KCP-vs-ENet comparison and the sample numbers; MIT, 16.9k stars and last commit 2026-06-23 confirmed. Shortcomings: informal single internet run, no hardware or loss rate, wiki excerpt is a cherry-picked bad moment; full logs show KCP wins tail latency (p99 574 vs 3,911 ms) but loses on median (80 vs 62 ms); TCP claim has no data.

tier_reason: Benchmark code is public (benchmark/throughput/evpp and benchmark/throughput/libevent/server.c, client.c, single_thread.sh, built by tools/benchmark-build.sh as a CMake Release build with -O3 -g -ggdb -DNDEBUG), and the page states gcc 4.8.2, CentOS 6.2 and Xeon E5-2630 v2; first-party but fully reproducible, so A by the tier rules.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Text: evpp throughput is about 17% higher than libevent2 when the message is smaller than 4096 bytes and about 40%~130% higher when larger. Chart tables (MB/s at 1/10/100/1000/10000 connections, one thread per side): 1024 B evpp 49.0/148.7/154.7/113.1/87.2 vs libevent 44.5/126.8/135.2/99.8/67.0 (1.10x-1.30x); 4096 B 176.7/512.0/527.4/382.3/293.7 vs 164.3/437.9/448.1/299.5/213.5 (1.08x-1.38x); 8192 B 318.1/880.1/902.8/612.0/505.4 vs 259.8/658.9/661.3/430.6/388.7 (1.22x-1.42x); 16384 B 513.8/1353.5/1297.0/877.8/725.4 vs 527.5/669.4/632.2/370.4/314.4 (0.97x at 1 connection, 2.02x-2.37x at 10+ connections) (ratios derived from page data). Same docs set: evpp 20%~50% faster than asio 1.10.8 on the IO-event benchmark, about 2% slower than raw libevent there; throughput vs asio similar (asio 5%~10% ahead at 10,000+ connections) and vs muduo similar.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark (full code, compiler, flags and CPU are public, so A by the tier rules) but old: CentOS 6.2, gcc 4.8.2 and libevent 2.0.21. The absolute numbers are in PNG charts with data tables hosted on raw.githubusercontent.com/zieckey/resources (the evpp author's own repo). The authors attribute the large-message gap to evpp's own buffer and to libevent reading at most 4096 bytes per read; that cap is EVBUFFER_MAX_READ hard-coded in libevent 2.0.21's evbuffer_read (a library limit, not just the sample), and current libevent master makes it configurable (evbuffer max_read, bufferevent_set_max_single_read with a 16384 bufferevent default), so the 2x gap at 16 KiB is specific to libevent 2.0.x and likely shrinks on newer libevent. With 16 KiB messages and a single connection evpp is about 3% slower (513.8 vs 527.5 MB/s); at 8192 bytes the gain is 22%-42%, below the stated 40%~130% band, while at 16384 it peaks at 137%. In the same docs set raw libevent is about 2% faster than evpp on the IO-event benchmark, and asio and muduo throughput are described as similar, so the win is over libevent 2.0's bufferevent layer specifically. Repo has had no commits since 2022-11-06. The README file is readme.md (lowercase), which is why raw README.md returned 404.

notes: Doc page, scripts, CMake flags, BSD-3-Clause, 3.8k stars and last commit 2022-11-06 (abandoned) confirmed; opened the chart PNGs for absolute numbers. Shortcomings: old toolchain and libevent 2.0.21; large-message win comes from libevent 2.0's hard-coded 4096-byte read cap (configurable in newer libevent); evpp 3% slower at 1 connection with 16 KiB messages; 8192-byte gains (22%-42%) fall below the stated 40%~130%.

tier_reason: Independent third-party suite with public scripts and raw wrk outputs, but the only baseline comparison is unequal: benchmarks/nginx/conf/echo.conf runs nginx with worker_processes 4 while benchmarks/kore/conf/kore.conf runs Kore with 12 workers on a 6-core/12-thread E5-1650 v2, with wrk on the same host; compiler and flags are unstated, so the 1.50x over nginx is not a like-for-like measurement and the record drops to C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Best of four 20 s wrk runs per framework: Kore 572,782 req/s (99% latency 3.99 ms) vs Nginx echo module 381,368 req/s (99% latency 24.24 ms), about 1.50x throughput (derived from page data); raw files show Kore 568,319-572,782 and nginx_echo 371,800-381,368 req/s across runs 02-04 and 01-04. Nginx ran 4 worker processes and Kore 12 workers, so the ratio is not like-for-like. Same table: libmicrohttpd 533,626, Undertow 616,547 (ahead of Kore), Go net/http 270,253, C++ Crow 256,552, Node HTTP 112,086 req/s.
corrections.hardware: Xeon E5-1650 v2 @ 3.50GHz (6 cores, 12 threads; results directory E5-1650v2-Ubuntu-14.04LTS), 32 GB RAM, Ubuntu 14.04 LTS, Linux 3.16; wrk ran on the same host over localhost
corrections.workload: Hello World text/plain response over HTTP/1.1 keep-alive on localhost, measuring framework overhead only: wrk with 12 threads (one per hardware thread), 100 connections, four 20 s runs per framework (time.sh), best run reported; Kore built with make NOTLS=1 and 12 workers, nginx (OpenResty build) with the echo module and 4 worker processes.
corrections.caveats: Independent third-party suite (nanoant/WebFrameworkBenchmark, MIT, public wrk script and raw results) but a single 2015 setup with an unequal baseline: benchmarks/nginx/conf/echo.conf sets worker_processes 4 while benchmarks/kore/conf/kore.conf sets workers 12 on a 12-thread CPU, and wrk's 12 threads share the same machine, so nginx was given a third of Kore's worker count (its 24 ms p99 is consistent with saturation). Nginx is OpenResty's binary (run_echo.sh) serving through the third-party echo module with more_clear_headers instead of a static response. Kore built without TLS (make NOTLS=1) from a very early 2015 Kore submodule; compiler and flags unstated. Undertow (Java) beat Kore in the same table. Later independent data is less flattering: the-benchmarker/web-frameworks (README at commit 37f10ec, updated 2020-05-06, wrk with 8 threads; not re-checked by this verifier) lists Kore 3.3 at 85,687 req/s with 64 connections, behind Go fasthttp 159,448 and gin 95,867, and has no nginx row. Kore's own README and GitHub page contain no performance numbers; the listing's claim word is only 'scalable'.

notes: Table numbers and raw wrk files match; ISC, 3.8k stars, last commit 2026-10-03 confirmed. Downgraded B to C because the nginx baseline ran 4 worker processes against Kore's 12 workers on a 12-thread box (crippled-baseline config, AssemblyScript precedent), wrk shared the host, and flags are unstated; no other Kore-vs-nginx data found.
